1184.title: Straw (6 December 1273)
1184.hook: after an experience at Mass he stops writing: all I've written seems like straw
1184.howItsDone: Catholics tell this story when speaking of Thomas, as a reminder that even the best theology falls short of God; the Summa itself is still studied in seminaries and universities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the crucifix in Naples: asked what reward he wanted, Thomas answered, nothing but you. Your line was only you, Lord.

A pen goes down on a desk and doesn't get picked up again. That's the whole scene. No fire, no vision on a mountain. As tradition tells it, Thomas Aquinas, in the middle of the third part of the Summa, the great book this block has been walking through, goes to Mass one morning in Naples. Something happens there. Afterward he stops writing, and he doesn't start again. His friends are alarmed. His companion Reginald keeps asking why.
screen: `A PEN GOES DOWN.` → `SOMETHING HAPPENS AT MASS.` → `REGINALD ASKS WHY.`

segments.voice: Tradition gives his answer like this. I can't, Reginald. Everything I have written seems to me like straw, compared with what I have seen. In Latin the word is palea: straw, or chaff, the dry husk left when the grain is gone. Nobody knows what Thomas saw. He didn't describe it, the people who passed the story down didn't claim to know, and it's better not to fill in the silence for him. What tradition does say is that the Summa was left unfinished. One easy reading is that his work was worthless, and he finally admitted it. Catholics haven't taken it that way. The Church went on to call him a Doctor of the Church and still teaches from his books. The point is the comparison. A map is straw next to the mountain. A letter is straw next to the person walking through the door. Thomas had written that what we say of God is true, but always falls short of him. Here he seems to have felt that falling short from the inside. Paul says something close, in the Douay-Rheims: "We see now through a glass in a dark manner; but then face to face." Some readers notice one more thing. Straw isn't nothing. It held the grain while it grew. So Thomas's words may be straw, and still worth carrying. And there's a quiet lesson in the stopping: a mind that had hardly ever stopped set the pen down, and rested in something bigger than its work.

segments.voice: Notice whatever task is pulling at you right now, the email, the dishes, the deadline, and let it sit on the desk for a little while; you'll pick it up again, though Thomas didn't. Let your hands go loose, and let your work be smaller than you, just for this sit. If you pray, rest in God without saying anything at all.

1185.title: Fossanova (1274)
1185.hook: he dies on the way to a council, aged about forty-nine
1185.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Thomas Aquinas, the Angelic Doctor, with Mass and sometimes with prayers for students and teachers, and some Catholic schools and universities honor him as a patron.

segments.voice: Yesterday, straw: Thomas set down his pen, and everything he'd written seemed like straw next to what he'd seen. Your line was like straw.

A letter arrives from the pope, the early accounts say. There's to be a great council of the Church in Lyon, in France, and Thomas is wanted there. So the man who has stopped writing gets on the road anyway, heading north from Naples with his companions. Somewhere along the way he falls ill and can't go on. The door that finally opens to him isn't a Dominican house. It belongs to white-robed Cistercian monks, in an abbey called Fossanova.
screen: `A LETTER FROM THE POPE.` → `ILL ON THE ROAD.` → `A DOOR AT FOSSANOVA.`

segments.voice: Tradition tells the last days quietly. The monks of Fossanova take him in. He's a stranger, a friar, not one of their own, and they nurse him anyway. Sick as he was, tradition says, he spoke to them about the Song of Songs, the love poem in the middle of the Bible. The great arguer, at the end, talking about love. At his last Communion, the early accounts give him words of deep faith in Christ present in the sacrament, the same faith as the Corpus Christi hymns tradition credits to him. Then he dies there, among Cistercians, far from Paris and the lecture halls, his great book unfinished. Paul, near his own end, says in the Douay-Rheims: "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith." Thomas didn't finish his Summa. Catholics would say he finished his course. After his death the Church named him a saint, and later a Doctor of the Church, a teacher for the whole Church. And Catholics gave him a nickname that stuck: the Angelic Doctor. People explain it in different ways. Some point to his careful writing on the angels. Others point to his life, which his companions remembered as pure and gentle, almost unearthly in its calm. Both reasons are told; neither is the whole of it. One more quiet detail: the friar who gave his life to teaching was cared for at the end by monks of a praying order.

1186.title: Many schools
1186.hook: Catholic thought also has Bonaventure, Scotus and many others; the Church keeps several schools
1186.howItsDone: Catholic universities and seminaries teach Thomas alongside Augustine, Bonaventure, Scotus and others, and theologians from different schools can debate open questions in print and in class.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Fossanova: Thomas, on the road to a council, taken in by Cistercian monks, and dying in their care. Your line was the angelic doctor.

After a whole block with one teacher, it's fair to wonder: is Thomas Aquinas simply what Catholics think? Is the Summa the official answer key, and everyone else a footnote? A Catholic university library tells another story. Next to Thomas sit Augustine, from long before; Bonaventure, a Franciscan who taught in Paris in Thomas's own time; John Duns Scotus, another Franciscan, who argued with Thomas's ideas after Thomas was gone. And more besides.
screen: `IS THOMAS THE ANSWER KEY?` → `THE SHELVES SAY OTHERWISE.` → `AUGUSTINE, BONAVENTURE, SCOTUS.`

segments.voice: A school, here, isn't a building. It's a way of thinking that teachers hand down to students, generation after generation. Thomists follow Thomas. Scotists follow Scotus. Others draw mainly on Augustine, or on Bonaventure. Each school has its favorite questions and its own instincts, its own way of putting God, the soul and the world together. Here's the surprising part. The Church has praised Thomas very highly and recommended him to students for the priesthood. But it has not made him the only teacher. On many questions it lets these schools disagree, out loud and in print, without naming a winner. Their students argue in classrooms and stay at the same altar. That's how Thomas wrote, too: in the Summa the other side always gets its say, stated fairly, before the answer. A school that learned from Thomas has to be ready to listen to one that didn't. Paul saw an early version of this. In Corinth, people were lining up behind favorite teachers, one for Paul, one for Apollo. Paul's answer, in the Douay-Rheims: "I have planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the increase." Teachers are gardeners. None of them owns the garden. So as this block closes, look back at what Thomas gave: a boy who kept his call, an argument that states the other side, grace that completes, God holding the world now, habits that make us, a lamp that lights others, and straw next to what he saw. One teacher, and many beside him.

If you pray, ask God to plant, water or grow something through a voice you'd never have chosen.

1187.title: Listen (Rule, Prologue)
1187.hook: the Rule begins with listen, with the ear of your heart
1187.howItsDone: Benedictine monks and nuns hear passages of the Rule read aloud in community, and oblates and other laypeople read it at home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, many schools: Thomas beside Augustine, Bonaventure and Scotus, kept side by side. Your line was many teachers.

Nod. Say mm-hm. Plan your reply while the other person is still talking. Half-listening takes almost no effort, and it can pass for the real thing for a long time. A new block begins today: the great religious orders, the communities of monks, friars and sisters who share a way of life. First, the Benedictines, and a small book written for monks in Italy long ago. Its very first word is not pray. Not work. Not obey. Listen.
screen: `HALF-LISTENING.` → `A NEW BLOCK: THE GREAT ORDERS.` → `THE FIRST WORD: LISTEN.`

segments.voice: Back on day eighty-seven you met Benedict and his sister Scholastica, his twin, tradition says. Tradition gives him the Rule, a short book to guide monks living together in Italy. Monks call it simply the Rule. It covers prayer and work, meals and sleep, guests and the sick, and how to settle a quarrel. But it opens like a letter from a father to a son. In Latin: inclina aurem cordis tui. Listen, my son, to the teaching of the master, and bend down the ear of your heart. It's the posture of someone leaning in to catch a quiet voice, a parent bent over a cot. And it's the ear of the heart, not just the ears on your head: letting what you hear reach the place where you decide things. The Prologue says this listening should turn into doing, and that the one speaking is finally God. It borrows a psalm, in the Douay-Rheims: "To day if you shall hear his voice, harden not your hearts." Notice the order. Before the long list of chapters, before the schedule, before a single bell rings, there's a posture: lean in. A rule, for Benedict, isn't a cage of instructions. It's a shared way of listening, kept day after day, so a whole community can hear together. Benedictine monks and nuns still read the Rule aloud together, and each time they come back around to its start, the first thing they hear is: listen.

1188.title: A school for beginners (Prologue)
1188.hook: Benedict hopes to set down nothing harsh or burdensome
1188.howItsDone: Benedictine communities welcome newcomers through a period of trial and learning, and Benedictines describe their whole life as a school of the Lord's service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Rule: Benedict's book for monks opens with one word, listen. Your line was the ear of the heart.

A bright sticker on the back of a car: student driver. The cars behind it soften. They give more room. They don't honk when it stalls at the light. The sticker doesn't make the driver any better. It just tells the truth: this person is learning, so be patient. Saint Benedict, near the end of the Prologue to his Rule, puts something like that sticker on the whole monastery.
screen: `STUDENT DRIVER.` → `THE CARS BEHIND GIVE ROOM.` → `BENEDICT'S STICKER.`

segments.voice: Benedict tells his monks what he's building. In Latin: dominici schola servitii, a school of the Lord's service. Not a fortress for the already holy. A school, a place where people come because they don't know yet. Then comes the hope that gives this day its line. In setting it up, he hopes to lay down nothing harsh, nothing heavy. He's honest, though: some things may feel a little strict, for good reasons, to correct faults and to protect love. When that happens, he asks the beginner not to run away in fear, because the way in is narrow at the start. Then a promise. As someone goes on in this life and in faith, the heart grows wider, and they run the way of God's commandments with a sweetness of love that's hard to put into words. That's the Rule borrowing a psalm, in the Douay-Rheims: "I have run the way of thy commandments, when thou didst enlarge my heart." Look at the shape of it. Narrow at the start, wider as you go. Strict in places, but never meant to crush. Benedict isn't writing for heroes; he's writing for people who will stall at the light. And at the very end of the Rule, he'll call the whole book, not just the first chapter, a little rule for beginners. In Benedict's school, nobody graduates.

1189.title: The abbot (ch. 2)
1189.hook: the abbot holds the place of Christ and must adapt to each person
1189.howItsDone: In Benedictine monasteries the monks elect their abbot or abbess, who leads the community and is responsible for each member's care, following chapter 2 of the Rule.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a school for beginners: Benedict hoped to set down nothing harsh or heavy. Your line was nothing harsh.

Should a good boss treat everyone the same? It sounds like fairness: same rules, same tone, same speech for the whole team. But a coach who barks at every player the same way loses some of them. One needs a push. One needs a joke. One needs to be left alone until Thursday. Saint Benedict's Rule has a chapter on the person in charge of the monastery, and it asks something harder than sameness.
screen: `TREAT EVERYONE THE SAME?` → `ONE NEEDS A PUSH, ONE A JOKE.` → `THE PERSON IN CHARGE.`

segments.voice: Chapter two starts high. The abbot is believed to hold the place of Christ in the monastery, because he's called by Christ's own name for the Father: abba. Benedict points to Paul, who says in the Douay-Rheims that we have received a spirit "whereby we cry: Abba (Father)." So abbot, in the Rule's own words, is a father's name. Then the chapter turns the weight around. Because he holds that place, the abbot will answer to God for every soul in his care. He's to teach more by what he does than by what he says. He's not to put a monk born free ahead of one who came from slavery. And he has to fit himself to each person: their character, their understanding. Coax one. Correct another. Reason with a third. Some respond to a gentle word; others need it said plainly. He should serve many temperaments, the Rule says, so that none of the flock is lost. Notice what Benedict isn't saying. The rules don't change for favorites. The same care wears different clothes for different people. Every monk gets the abbot's full attention, not the same speech. The Rule knows it's hard, calling the role difficult and demanding work: ruling souls. A father's name, a heavy account, and a habit of looking at each face before speaking.

1190.title: Taking counsel (ch. 3)
1190.hook: the whole community is called, because God often reveals the better way to the youngest
1190.howItsDone: In Benedictine monasteries the abbot or abbess consults the community in chapter before major decisions, as chapter 3 of the Rule describes, and then makes the decision.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the abbot: a father's name, holding the place of Christ, fitting his care to each person. Your line was each one differently. Today closes the week.

The grown-ups have been going around in circles all evening: which car to sell, how to fit the move around school, who takes the dog. Then the youngest at the table, spooning up a bowl of cereal, says the obvious thing nobody had seen. The room goes quiet. Somebody laughs. And it's right, and everyone at the table knows it. Saint Benedict built that moment into the life of a monastery, on purpose.
screen: `GOING AROUND IN CIRCLES.` → `THE YOUNGEST SAYS IT.` → `BENEDICT BUILDS IT IN.`

segments.voice: Chapter three of the Rule is short. Whenever something important has to be decided, the abbot calls the whole community together and tells them what's at stake. Everyone, not just the senior monks. He listens to their advice, thinks it over on his own, and does what he judges best. And here's Benedict's reason for calling everyone: the Lord often shows what is better to the younger. The newest monk, the one with the least standing, may be the one who sees it. He tells the monks how to speak up: humbly, without stubbornly defending their own view. And he tells the abbot he'll answer to God for what he decides, so he should decide fairly. The final call is still his. This isn't a vote. It's something quieter: a leader who has to hear the whole room before he chooses. The Bible has a story that fits. In the temple, God's voice comes in the night, not to the old priest Eli, but to the boy Samuel. Eli tells him how to answer, and the boy says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth." Look back at this week: Thomas's straw and his last days at Fossanova, many schools beside him, then Benedict's first word, listen; a school for beginners; an abbot who fits himself to each person; and now an abbot who listens to the youngest. A whole week about who gets heard.
screen: `CALL THE WHOLE COMMUNITY.` · `GOD SHOWS THE YOUNGER WHAT'S BETTER.` · `SPEAK HUMBLY; THE ABBOT DECIDES.` · `A WEEK ABOUT WHO GETS HEARD.` · then, large: `SPEAK, LORD, FOR THY SERVANT HEARETH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a decision you're carrying, big or small, and then someone younger or newer than you: a child, a niece, a new hire, a friend just starting out. Put the question the way you'd put it to them, one plain sentence with no background, and notice what drops away when it has to be that simple. If you pray, ask God to speak to you through whoever you least expect.
Taking counsel. In Benedict's Rule, the abbot calls the whole community before an important decision, because the Lord often shows what is better to the younger. Today's word.
Your line: the youngest may be right. Sometimes the clearest voice in the room is the newest one. That's the week.
